topic: DP-3T: The Privacy-First Contact Tracing Algorithm
target_audience: University students and technology enthusiasts interested in cybersecurity and privacy.

sections.title: The Privacy Paradox
lecture_lines: Contact tracing stops virus spread but risks privacy.
Centralized systems can track every movement via GPS.
We must track proximity without using surveillance.
Alice and Bob meet without sharing their location.
How can Alice be notified if Bob gets sick?
animations: Show a map icon in center; color corresponding lecture line.
Show 'Big Brother' eye icon looking at a GPS pin on a phone.
Cross out the eye and GPS pin with red '#FF0000' lines.
Show Alice (#FFD700) and Bob (#ADD8E6) silhouettes meeting in a park.
Display a question mark above Alice to represent the notification paradox.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Cryptographic Hashing
lecture_lines: Hash functions create unique fingerprints for any input.
They are one-way, meaning you cannot reverse them.
This ensures original data remains hidden and secure.
animations: Display a 'Meat Grinder' icon labeled 'HASH' in center.
A Key ($K$) enters the grinder and a Hash string ($H$) emerges.
Show a red '#FF0000' arrow trying and failing to reverse the hash.

sections.title: Step 1: Daily Keys and Ephemeral IDs
lecture_lines: Each day, the phone generates a Secret Day Key.
From this, it derives multiple short-term Ephemeral IDs.
These IDs change every fifteen minutes for privacy.
animations: Show a golden 'Secret Day Key' ($SK_t$) icon (#FFD700).
Generate multiple 'Ephemeral ID' tags from the Secret Day Key.
Show a timer icon rotating as the ID tags cycle every 15 minutes.

sections.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Chirping)
lecture_lines: Phones use Bluetooth to "chirp" their current ID.
Nearby phones listen and record these random IDs.
Both phones store exchanged IDs in a local logbook.
animations: Position Alice's phone (#FFD700) and Bob's phone (#ADD8E6) near each other.
Animate Bluetooth waves 'chirping' random IDs between the two devices.
Show the IDs being written into a 'Local Logbook' on each phone.

sections.title: Step 3: The Diagnosis and Report
lecture_lines: A positive user uploads only their Secret Day Keys.
They do not upload contact lists or location history.
The central server hosts these keys on a bulletin.
animations: Change Bob's phone color to red (#FF0000) for a positive diagnosis.
Animate Bob's 'Secret Day Keys' moving to a central cloud server.
Display the keys on a 'Public Bulletin Board' icon.

sections.title: Step 4: Decentralized Verification
lecture_lines: Phones download new Secret Day Keys from the server.
Each phone regenerates the IDs from those secret keys.
It compares these IDs against its local logbook.
A match indicates proximity to an infected person.
Users receive alerts without the server knowing who matched.
animations: Alice's phone downloads 'Secret Day Keys' from the public server.
Inside the phone, the key generates all possible EphIDs.
Open Alice's 'Local Logbook' to show previously stored IDs.
Highlight a matching ID pair in green (#00FF00) with a pulse effect.
Display an 'Exposure Notification' alert on Alice's screen.

sections.title: Summary: Security by Design
lecture_lines: DP-3T ensures the server remains "blind" to encounters.
Data flows to users without returning personal info.
Alice's identity remains protected inside a locked box.
The system is decentralized to ensure maximum privacy.
Technology proves that privacy and safety can coexist.
animations: Show the central server with a blindfold icon to represent anonymity.
Animate data flowing outward to users without returning personal info.
Display Alice's identity as a locked box (#FFFFFF).
Boldly display the word 'DECENTRALIZED' in green (#00FF00).
Group icons of a Lock, Phone, and Heart to represent private safety.
